```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
library(survival)
library(survminer)
library(gt)
library(knitr)

# --- Load and clean (same pipeline as the paper) ---------------------
data_raw <- read_csv("ipr_dataset.csv", na = c("", "NA"))

empty_cols <- names(data_raw)[colSums(is.na(data_raw)) == nrow(data_raw)]
data <- data_raw %>% select(-all_of(empty_cols))

df <- data %>%
  mutate(
    event        = as.integer(is_recid),
    release_date = as.Date(exit_sup_end_date),
    time_days    = if_else(event == 1L, days_to_recid, 1095)
  ) %>%
  mutate(time_days = if_else(time_days == 0, 0.5, time_days)) %>%
  unite("exit_combined", exit_type, exit_subtype, sep = " - ", remove = FALSE) %>%
  filter(!is.na(sex)) %>%
  mutate(
    sex             = factor(sex),
    Race            = factor(Race),
    exit_type       = factor(exit_type),
    exit_sup_reason = factor(exit_sup_reason),
    risk_ranking    = factor(
      if_else(is.na(risk_ranking), "Not Assessed", risk_ranking),
      levels = c("Low", "Moderate", "High", "Not Assessed")
    ),
    age_c = age - mean(age, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# --- Models ----------------------------------------------------------
cox_model <- coxph(
  Surv(time_days, event) ~ age_c + sex + risk_ranking + exit_type + exit_sup_reason,
  data = df
)

cox_strat <- coxph(
  Surv(time_days, event) ~ age_c + sex + risk_ranking + exit_type +
    strata(exit_sup_reason),
  data = df
)

zph_init  <- cox.zph(cox_model)
zph_strat <- cox.zph(cox_strat)
```


## The Question {.smaller}

- Roughly **one in three** people released from Iowa prisons returns within three years.

- Two people can both return within that window — one after **30 days**, the other after **two years**.

- A yes/no measure counts those identically.


**If we only ask *whether* reincarceration happened, we miss when it happened — and when is what reentry programming has to plan around.**
. . .

---

## Why Timing Matters

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**A binary outcome tells you:**

- How many returned
- Who returned

Analyzed with logistic regression
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**A time-to-event outcome tells you:**

- How many returned
- Who returned
- **When** they returned
- What happens to people still at risk

Analyzed with survival analysis
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Our question: which demographic, risk, offense, and release characteristics are associated with the **hazard** of reincarceration — and do those associations hold steady over three years?
:::

. . .

---

## The Data {.smaller}

**Iowa Prison Recidivism Status** — Iowa Department of Corrections, via data.iowa.gov

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- **31,703** case-level release records
- Release cohorts **FY2016 – FY2022**
- Parole, work release, or discharge
- Uniform **three-year** tracking window
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
**Variables used**

- Age at release
- Sex, race
- Risk classification
- Offense type
- Release supervision reason
- Days to reincarceration
:::
:::

**Analysis sample:** 31,700 records (3 removed for missing sex) · **11,699 events (36.9%)**

. . .


---

## Defining Time and Censoring {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
- Clock starts at **release**
- Event = return to prison
- No return by the end of follow-up → **right-censored at 1,095 days**
- 6 same-day returns set to 0.5 days so they stay in the risk set
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r swimmer, fig.height=4.2}
set.seed(42)
pt <- df %>%
  slice_sample(n = 20) %>%
  arrange(time_days) %>%
  mutate(id = row_number())

ggplot(pt, aes(y = id)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = time_days, yend = id),
               colour = "#3a86d4", linewidth = 1.4) +
  geom_point(aes(x = time_days,
                 shape = factor(event), colour = factor(event)),
             size = 3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1095, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("0" = 62, "1" = 19),
                     labels = c("Censored", "Reincarcerated")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("0" = "#3a86d4", "1" = "#d1495b"),
                      labels = c("Censored", "Reincarcerated")) +
  labs(x = "Days since release", y = NULL,
       shape = NULL, colour = NULL,
       title = "20 randomly sampled records") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom")
```
:::
:::

## When Do Returns Happen? {.smaller}

```{r event-timing, fig.height=3.6, fig.width=9}
df %>%
  filter(event == 1) %>%
  mutate(month = pmin(ceiling(time_days / 30.44), 36)) %>%
  count(month) %>%
  ggplot(aes(month, n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#d1495b", width = 0.85) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 36, 6)) +
  labs(x = "Months since release", y = "Reincarcerations",
       title = "Monthly reincarceration counts among the 11,699 who returned") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

- Returns are **rare in month one**, then climb sharply
- Peak around **months 6–7** (~570 per month)
- Decline to roughly **150 per month** by the end of follow-up
- Mean time to reincarceration: **449 days**

## Release Pathway Matters Most {.smaller}

```{r pathway-rates}
df %>%
  group_by(exit_sup_reason) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), Rate = 100 * mean(event), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(Rate)) %>%
  rename(`Release reason` = exit_sup_reason, N = n) %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(columns = Rate, decimals = 1) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = N, use_seps = TRUE, decimals = 0) %>%
  cols_label(Rate = "3-yr rate (%)") %>%
  tab_options(table.font.size = "70%")
```

## Kaplan–Meier Curves {.smaller}

```{r km-plots, fig.height=4.4, fig.width=10}
library(patchwork)

pal3 <- c("#257de0", "#00b894", "#ec4647")  # low → high hazard
pal2 <- c("#257de0", "#ec4647")

km_panel <- function(data, var, labs, title, cols) {
  fit <- surv_fit(as.formula(paste("Surv(time_days, event) ~", var)),
                  data = data)
  ggsurvplot(
    fit, data = data,
    conf.int = FALSE, linetype = "strata",
    legend = "bottom", legend.title = "", legend.labs = labs,
    palette = cols, title = title,
    xlab = "Days", ylab = NULL,
    ggtheme = theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
  )$plot +
    theme(plot.title   = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
          legend.text  = element_text(size = 8),
          legend.margin = margin(t = -4))
}

# --- Risk: Low vs High (Moderate is intermediate; Not Assessed noted verbally)
d_risk <- df %>% filter(risk_ranking %in% c("Low", "High")) %>%
  mutate(risk_ranking = droplevels(risk_ranking))

# --- Offense: best, model reference, worst
d_off <- df %>% filter(exit_type %in% c("Violent", "Drug", "Other")) %>%
  mutate(exit_type = factor(exit_type, levels = c("Violent", "Drug", "Other")))

# --- Release: best, largest, worst
d_rel <- df %>% filter(exit_sup_reason %in% c(
    "Discharged - Expiration of Sentence", "Parole Granted",
    "Released to Special Sentence")) %>%
  mutate(exit_sup_reason = factor(exit_sup_reason, levels = c(
    "Discharged - Expiration of Sentence", "Parole Granted",
    "Released to Special Sentence")))

p1 <- km_panel(d_risk, "risk_ranking", c("Low", "High"),
               "Risk classification", pal2)
p2 <- km_panel(d_off, "exit_type", c("Violent", "Drug", "Other"),
               "Offense type", pal3)
p3 <- km_panel(df, "sex", c("Female", "Male"), "Sex", pal2)
p4 <- km_panel(d_rel, "exit_sup_reason",
               c("Expiration", "Parole granted", "Special sentence"),
               "Release reason", pal3)

(p1 | p2) / (p3 | p4)
```
*Selected categories shown for legibility; full results in the hazard ratio tables*

## Log-Rank Tests

| Comparison | χ² | df | *p* |
|------------|---:|---:|----:|
| Release reason | 1,254.57 | 7 | <0.001 |
| Offense type | 527.04 | 4 | <0.001 |
| Risk classification | 367.29 | 3 | <0.001 |
| Sex | 98.53 | 1 | <0.001 |


These are **unadjusted** comparisons — they don't account for relationships among the predictors. That motivates a multivariable model.

. . .

---

## The Cox Proportional Hazards Model {.smaller}

$$
\lambda(t \mid X) = \lambda_0(t)\exp(\beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \cdots + \beta_p X_p)
$$

- $\lambda_0(t)$ is the **baseline hazard**, left unspecified — no distributional assumption about survival times
- $\beta_j$ is a regression coefficient; $X_j$ an explanatory variable


$$
\text{HR}_j = \exp(\beta_j)
$$

- **HR > 1** → higher hazard of reincarceration
- **HR < 1** → lower hazard
- **HR = 1** → no difference



::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**The core assumption:** the hazard ratio for a predictor stays constant across the whole follow-up period.
:::

. . .

---

## Initial Cox Model: Who {.smaller}

31,700 records · 11,699 events · LR χ² = 2,776.51, df = 16, *p* < 0.001 · **concordance = 0.638**

| Predictor | HR | 95% CI |
|-----------|---:|--------|
| Age (per year) | 0.986 | 0.984 – 0.987 |
| Male (vs. female) | 1.289 | 1.216 – 1.367 |
| Moderate risk (vs. low) | 1.180 | — |
| High risk (vs. low) | 1.515 | — |
| Not assessed (vs. low) | 0.867 | 0.774 – 0.972 |
| Violent offense (vs. drug) | 0.617 | 0.583 – 0.653 |


- Each additional year of age → **1.4% lower** hazard
- High-risk classification → **51.5% higher** hazard than low risk
- Violent offenses → **38.3% lower** hazard than drug offenses
. . .

---

## Initial Cox Model: Release Pathway {.smaller}

Reference: discharged at expiration of sentence

| Release reason | HR | 95% CI |
|----------------|---:|--------|
| Released to special sentence | 2.83 | 2.57 – 3.12 |
| Paroled to Iowa detainer | 2.60 | 2.19 – 3.08 |
| Parole granted | 1.89 | 1.80 – 1.99 |
| Paroled to out-of-state detainer | 1.02 | *p* = 0.871 |
| Paroled w/ immediate discharge | 0.72 | 0.62 – 0.83 |
| U.S. Marshal detainer | 0.15 | — |
| INS detainer | 0.11 | — |


Release pathway produced the **largest** differences in the model — but these are associations, not evidence that release arrangements cause or prevent return.

. . .

---

## The Assumption Fails {.smaller}

Scaled Schoenfeld residual tests on the initial model:

| Term | χ² | *p* |
|------|---:|----:|
| **Global** | **437.69** | **<0.001** |
| Release reason | 370.66 | <0.001 |
| Risk classification | 31.01 | <0.001 |
| Offense type | 22.81 | <0.001 |
| Sex | 7.89 | 0.005 |
| Age | — | 0.115 |


Several predictor effects **vary over follow-up**. A single hazard ratio may not describe them well — exactly what Bellera et al. [-@bellera2010] warn about.

Release reason showed the strongest violation → **stratify on it**.

. . .

---

## Stratified Cox Model {.smaller}

Separate baseline hazard for each release category; shared coefficients for everything else.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Estimates barely moved**

| Predictor | Initial | Stratified |
|-----------|--------:|-----------:|
| Age | 0.986 | 0.986 |
| Male | 1.289 | 1.290 |
| High risk | 1.515 | 1.511 |
| Violent | 0.617 | 0.617 |
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**PH test after stratification**

| Term | Before | After |
|------|-------:|------:|
| Global | 437.69 | **67.15** |
| Risk | 31.01 | 8.63 |
| Offense | 22.81 | **50.49** |
:::
:::


- Global statistic dropped sharply — stratification helped
- But it **did not resolve** the violation: global *p* < 0.001
- Offense type's violation got **worse**

. . .

---

## What This Means {.smaller}

- **Older age and female sex** were associated with lower hazard; **high-risk classification** with higher hazard.

- **Release pathway** showed the largest differences, though federal detainer groups likely reflect unobservable out-of-state returns.

- **The methodological finding is the real result:** statistically significant coefficients do not mean the model is adequate.

- Remaining hazard ratios should be read as **summary estimates across follow-up**, not constant relative hazards at every time point.

- Concordance of **0.638** — modest. Post-release employment, housing, and treatment access are not in these data.

---

## Limitations {.smaller}

- **Individual identifiers are fully redacted**, so we cannot verify whether one person contributes multiple release records — a possible violation of the independence assumption.

- **Follow-up duration could not be verified.** Censoring at 1,095 days is an analytical assumption, not confirmed event-free observation.

- **Recidivism is the agency's definition** — return to prison for any reason, combining new offenses with technical violations.

- **Out-of-jurisdiction returns are invisible**, which almost certainly explains the very low detainer-group hazards.

- Stratification addressed one violating predictor; **others remain**.

---

## Conclusion {.smaller}

- Among 31,700 Iowa release records, **36.9%** ended in reincarceration, with returns peaking **6–7 months** after release.

- Age, sex, risk classification, offense type, and release pathway were all associated with the hazard of return.

- **The proportional hazards assumption was violated**, and stratification only partly addressed it.

- Timing matters: *whether* someone returns and *when* they return are different questions, and only the second can inform when to deploy supervision and reentry resources.



**Next steps:** predictor-by-time interactions, competing-risk methods for out-of-jurisdiction transfers, and verified individual follow-up durations.

. . .
